calibration_status: SINGLE-ANCHOR CALIBRATION (n=1). The coefficients below are fitted to ONE delivered BMad project — EPP Phase 1: 76 stories across 9 epics, 540 h actual, split dev 280 / UX 120 / QA 40 / BA 40 / DevOps 30 / architect 30. That is far better than the reasoned hypothesis it replaces and far weaker than a trend: one project cannot separate what is true of BMad delivery from what is true of EPP. Say n=1 whenever a client asks how these numbers were arrived at. est-calibrate replaces them as more projects close.

calibration_history.why: The seeded model priced EPP at 3,147.5 h against 540 h actual — 5.83x. Two errors multiplied. The bands described a feature while the module prices a story, worth about 3x; and review, spec and QA rates assumed a human reading human-written output, while EPP ran an agent review pass per story, worth about 2x. Both were fitted against EPP's per-role actuals rather than loaded onto one coefficient, because a single scale that reproduces the total leaves every individual number indefensible. Re-priced: 569 h against 540 h actual, 1.05x, with every role within 1.2x except UX (0.74x, EPP included building a design system) and architect (1.89x, whose recorded 30 h explicitly excludes ongoing support the source notes would add 30-60 h).

_reading_this_file: Each coefficient is a three-point estimate (lo / likely / hi) plus a 'why' saying what it encodes. Change a value by editing it here — nothing in the skill hardcodes a number. Every estimate snapshots this whole file into its ledger entry, so a later change never rewrites the past.

size_bands._what: manual_baseline in hours: what this STORY would have cost a human team writing it by hand. NOT the BMad effort — the model derives that; conflating the two double-counts the compression. The unit is a story, not a feature: the priced item is one coherent unit of delivery, and these bands were three times too large while they still described a feature. EPP Phase 1: 76 delivered stories, 9 epics, 540 h actual (dev 280 / UX 120 / QA 40 / BA 40 / DevOps 30 / architect 30). n=1.

_anchor.source: One delivered multi-surface SaaS platform: 76 stories over 9 epics, 609 acceptance criteria, reconciled against 540 h of recorded actuals across six roles.
_anchor.why: The shape a band assignment is compared against, not a rule it must obey. M is the median story; L is a quarter of the work and it is the first-of-its-kind quarter; nothing in 76 delivered stories was small enough to be XS, and nothing was left XL. Read it as a reference class to argue with — n=1, and a data-migration or design-led engagement will legitimately sit elsewhere. What it is for: an inventory claiming 37% L is claiming that a third of the product is a capability the codebase has never had, and that claim should be made out loud rather than by accident.
_anchor.not_the_discriminator: Acceptance-criterion count does not separate the bands. In the anchor the first-OIDC story carries 4 acceptance criteria and is L; a routine configuration screen carries 7 and is M. Volume of stated requirement holds at the level of a whole inventory and fails story by story.

XS.why: A config change, a copy edit, one field on an existing form — usually a task, not a story
exemplars: A config value, a copy fix, one field on a form that already exists
None of the anchor's 76 delivered stories was XS. Something this small is normally a task inside a story, not a story — if a whole inventory carries XS rows, the unit is probably wrong

S.why: A single endpoint, a simple form, one static page, one report column
exemplars: A language pack against an i18n framework that already exists
A microcopy or tone pass over screens already built
A placeholder route behind a feature flag
One report column, one export, one static page

M.why: One story: an endpoint plus its screen, a documented integration point, a single multi-step flow
exemplars: A second entity's CRUD plus its configuration screen
A list and its detail view over one resource
Another path through a flow that already exists — a manual override beside the automated one
Profile create-and-edit over an account model already in place
A documented third-party API called for the first time, where the transport is already there
not_exemplars: Not S because a second entity still needs its own rules, its own screens and its own tests — the pattern is free, the specifics are not

L.why: The first of its kind in this codebase: a protocol, a transport, an external system, a framework, or a foundation everything after it is built on. The second story that uses that capability is M
exemplars: The first OIDC/SAML integration in the codebase — a new protocol, and both clients
An append-only ledger behind a hosted checkout, credited only on the verified webhook
The first real-time transport: sockets plus a broker
The first native device capability — camera scanning on a staff app
The i18n framework itself, before any language pack rides on it
The first outbound sync to an external system, with its retry and dead-letter path
The repository scaffold, or the design system, that everything after it is built on
not_exemplars: Not CRUD over one entity, however central the entity is to the product
Not a list plus its detail view, however many other features read from it
Not a derived read the whole product depends on — size it as the query it is; its reach is review_tier's business, and charging for reach here bills it twice

XL.why: A story that should have been split — a subsystem tracked as one row. The band is wide because an XL tag means the scope was never decomposed, and the estimate says so rather than pretending otherwise
exemplars: A catalogue of ~60 rules evaluated as one mechanism, where the source genuinely gives nothing to split on
Nothing in the anchor was left XL. est-estimate prices a narrowing question for every XL rather than treating the band as an answer

compressibility._what: How many times faster BMad builds this than a human team would. Divides manual_baseline to give build_h. This is the axis that separates an AI-delivery estimate from a conventional one. CALIBRATION NOTE: roughly double the seeded figures. EPP Phase 1 delivered 76 stories against a manual-equivalent baseline of about 1,200 h in 540 h all-in — a whole-project compression of 6.9x, which only reconciles with a build compression well above it, since review, QA and planning compress far less. n=1.

high.why: CRUD, greenfield screens, scaffolding, well-documented APIs, tests, docs, config — thoroughly represented in the model's world, so generation is near-free

medium.why: Conventional business logic, common integrations, standard mobile screens

low.why: Undocumented legacy, client-proprietary systems, bespoke algorithms, dirty-data migration, pixel-level craft — the effort is discovery, and discovery does not compress

none.why: Workshops, approvals, compliance sign-off, third-party lead times, experimental ML iteration — work where no code is the deliverable

review_rate._what: review_h as a share of manual_baseline — deliberately NOT of build_h. Review effort scales with the volume of output produced, not the time taken to produce it, so compression shrinks the build and leaves the review untouched. This single choice is why a payments feature stays expensive while CRUD collapses, with no special-casing anywhere. CALIBRATION NOTE: these rates are roughly half the manual-era figures because this company runs a fresh-context agent review pass per story before a human reads it. The STRUCTURE is unchanged — review is still a share of manual_baseline, so sensitive work still stays expensive relative to CRUD — but the level now reflects a human reading already-reviewed output. EPP Phase 1: 76 delivered stories, 9 epics, 540 h actual (dev 280 / UX 120 / QA 40 / BA 40 / DevOps 30 / architect 30). n=1.

routine.why: Feature delegated whole; a spot-review of the blast-radius surfaces only — DB migrations, tests, CI/CD

sensitive.why: Money, personal data, authentication and authorization: read line by line before anyone signs their name to it

critical.why: Regulated data, irreversible financial effects, safety: line-by-line plus an external or compliance sign-off that runs on someone else's calendar

clarity._what: spec_rate and rework_rate as shares of manual_baseline and of (build+review) respectively, plus band_multiplier, which widens the story's own interval. Under BMad, ambiguity is no longer resolved by a developer stopping to ask — it gets confidently implemented, reviewed, and rebuilt. Vagueness costs MORE than it did in manual delivery, which inverts the usual assumption. Rates are about half the manual-era figures for the same reason review is: the agent drafts the specification and catches its own first-pass mistakes. The ordering is untouched — vagueness still costs more under BMad, not less. BAND: without band_multiplier the spread ran BACKWARDS — holding size at M, a real inventory produced hi/lo of 6.32 at high clarity and 5.52 at low, because spec and rework are scalar multiples of an interval and therefore proportionally tight, so adding more of them pulled the ratio down. A vague story read as more certain than a specified one, which is the opposite of the signal the range exists to carry. The multiplier widens the total around its likely value, the same way uncertainty.completeness_multiplier does at project level — correlated risk, not independent noise. DOUBLE COUNT, measured: clarity is also 18% of input_completeness, which widens the PROJECT band, so the same signal is read twice. The overlap turns out to be immaterial — per-story sds combine in quadrature, so the aggregate barely moves: a project of uniformly high-clarity stories is unchanged to the decimal, a realistic mix moves 0.0pp, and one of entirely low-clarity stories widens 0.8pp. Nothing was removed from the completeness path, because there was nothing material to remove. EPP Phase 1: 76 delivered stories, 9 epics, 540 h actual (dev 280 / UX 120 / QA 40 / BA 40 / DevOps 30 / architect 30). n=1.

high.band_multiplier_why: Acceptance criteria present, data model implied, edge cases named — the interval the size band and compressibility already imply needs no widening
high.why: Acceptance criteria present, data model implied, edge cases named

medium.band_multiplier_why: Clear in prose, intent unambiguous, details absent. The details are where the hours hide, so the spread widens by an exponent on hi/lo
medium.why: Clear in prose, intent unambiguous, details absent

low.band_multiplier_why: A line in a transcript, or inferred from context. What is being built is genuinely not yet known, and a narrow band here would be false precision
low.why: A line in a transcript, or inferred from context. The rework rate is the dominant term here and it is real, not padding

standard.why: The team has built something of this shape before

novel.why: New to the team or genuinely uncommon. Novelty drives loops rather than build effort — the first attempt at an unfamiliar shape rarely converges in one pass

team_profiles._what: Modifiers on human-effort components only. build_h is left alone because the agent writes the code either way — the seniority gap lands entirely in the judgement-heavy work, and under BMad that gap widens rather than narrows.

senior-heavy.why: Sharper specs, faster sensitive-tier review, fewer loops to converge

balanced.why: The baseline the other profiles are relative to

junior-heavy.why: Review is slower and less reliable, and more loops are needed — the cost lands hardest where BMad concentrates human effort

new-to-bmad.why: A learning-curve modifier independent of seniority. Decays over the first few projects; est-calibrate should retire it per team once actuals show it has

planning._what: The BMad planning pipeline. planning_review_h is the estimate's high-confidence anchor because this company reviews 100% of planning artefacts without exception — it is a predictable function of scope volume rather than a guess, and its bands are correspondingly tight.
planning.features_per_epic_why: Fallback only, for an inventory whose stories carry no epic. EPP ran 76 stories across 9 epics — 8.4 per epic. The seeded 5 over-counted epics by 1.7x wherever it was reached.
planning.stories_per_feature_why: The priced item is a story, so it counts as one; only a genuinely under-decomposed row splits further. The seeded 1/1/2/4/8 dated from when a feature was the unit and turned EPP's 76 real stories into 178 modelled ones, inflating every planning figure derived from the count.

agent_hours._what: Human time steering the BMad workflow that authors each artefact — already compressed, since the agent drafts.

review_hours._what: Human time READING every planning artefact, end to end, no exceptions. Bands are deliberately tight — tighter than anything else in this model — because this is the one component the company performs identically on every project. It is reading at a known rate over a known volume, so the uncertainty is in the volume, not the rate. Report it with a visibly narrower range: it is the part of the number that can be defended hardest, and its tightness is the evidence for that claim rather than a rhetorical flourish.

documents_by_granularity.why: A whole project pays the full planning pipeline once. An epic inside a running project inherits the brief and UX and pays only for its own requirements and technical design. A sprint or single feature pays neither — the planning artefacts already exist.

standing_work._what: Work every project pays and no client document describes. It used to be one opaque `env_infra` lookup — 13.7 hours for a multi-tenant SaaS with payments, calendar sync and bulk imports, which nobody could defend because there was nothing inside it to point at. Each item below is priced through the same engine as any story, so it carries a band, a role split and a line in the feature table, and a client can argue with it item by item instead of being handed a number. Items are selected by the `stacks` list against the --stack profile; `all` means every project pays it. Suppress the whole section with --no-standing-work when the client is bringing an existing platform. Each item's tags carry their own per-axis reason, like any other classification: a single sentence repeated across five axes is the boilerplate pattern inventory-check.py reports, and shipping it in the catalogue would be holding the module to a standard the model itself did not meet. Items carry absolute `hours` rather than a size band: a pipeline costs what it costs however the product backlog is sliced, and while these resolved through the band table a re-scale of that table silently re-priced the whole catalogue with it.

repo_scaffold.name: Repository scaffold and shared configuration
repo_scaffold.why: Repo or monorepo layout, shared TypeScript/lint/format config, commit hooks, the test harness everything else is written against. Generated quickly, but the decisions in it are load-bearing for every story that follows.

reasons.compressibility: The shape is conventional and generates well, but the choices are load-bearing and get read
reasons.review_tier: No money, no personal data — a spot-check of the config that ships
reasons.clarity: The stack decides it; there is nothing ambiguous left once that is chosen
reasons.hours: A day or two of decisions that everything after inherits

bmad_setup.name: BMad setup and project context
bmad_setup.why: Installing the module set, writing project-context, customising the agents to this codebase's conventions. No code is the deliverable, so nothing compresses — but it is real hours on every BMad project and pretending otherwise makes the first sprint look faster than it is.

reasons.compressibility: No code is the deliverable, so nothing compresses
reasons.review_tier: Configuration of a working process, not of anything a client depends on
reasons.novelty: Routine for a team already running BMad
reasons.hours: An afternoon of installation and project-context writing

ci_pipeline.name: Build, test and deploy pipeline
ci_pipeline.why: Pipeline per environment, caching, migrations in the deploy, preview builds. Low compressibility because the work is configuration against real systems with real credentials, and an agent cannot click through a cloud console.

reasons.compressibility: Configuration against real systems with real credentials; an agent cannot click through a cloud console
reasons.review_tier: It deploys, but it holds no data of its own
reasons.clarity: The stack and the hosting decide almost all of it
reasons.novelty: A shape the team has built before
reasons.hours: A pipeline per environment, with caching, migrations and preview builds

environments.name: Environment provisioning and secrets
environments.why: Staging and production provisioning, DNS and TLS, secret storage and rotation. Sensitive tier because a mistake here exposes production credentials, and that is read line by line before anyone signs their name to it.

reasons.compressibility: Provisioning is manual work against consoles and providers
reasons.review_tier: A mistake here exposes production credentials, so it is read line by line
reasons.clarity: The hosting choice settles the work
reasons.hours: Staging and production, with DNS, TLS and secret storage

observability.name: Logging, metrics and alerting
observability.why: Structured logs, error tracking, the handful of alerts someone will actually act on. Cheap to generate, and the first thing dropped from an estimate that has no line for it.

reasons.compressibility: Instrumentation is generated well once the libraries are chosen
reasons.review_tier: Watches the system rather than holding anything
reasons.clarity: Well understood; the only open question is what to alert on
reasons.hours: Structured logs, error tracking and the few alerts anyone will act on

release_process.name: Release, rollback and migration process
release_process.why: Versioning, forward-only migrations, a rollback that has been rehearsed rather than assumed. Sensitive because the first time it is exercised is usually the worst possible time.

reasons.compressibility: The rehearsal is the work, and rehearsals do not compress
reasons.review_tier: The first time it is exercised is usually the worst possible time
reasons.hours: Versioning, forward-only migrations and a rehearsed rollback

mobile_release.name: Store provisioning and release channels
mobile_release.why: Signing identities, store listings, TestFlight and Play tracks, review turnaround. Runs on someone else's calendar, so it compresses not at all.

reasons.compressibility: Store review runs on someone else's calendar
reasons.review_tier: Process and credentials, not product data
reasons.novelty: Routine for a team that ships mobile
reasons.hours: Signing identities, store listings, and the tracks releases go out on

service_integration_env.name: Cross-service integration environment
service_integration_env.why: An environment where the services actually talk to each other, with inter-service auth and seeded data. Routinely omitted at estimate time and routinely the reason integration slips.

reasons.compressibility: Making several deployables agree is discovery work
reasons.review_tier: A test environment; nothing real passes through it
reasons.clarity: Depends on service boundaries that are usually still settling
reasons.hours: An environment where the services actually talk, with inter-service auth and seeded data

qa._what: qa_h as a share of total manual_baseline. Test generation compresses well; running, triaging and re-running does not. Rates are a quarter of the industry defaults: generated suites plus AI-assisted triage. EPP spent 40 h of QA against a manual baseline of roughly 1,200 h at story scale. EPP Phase 1: 76 delivered stories, 9 epics, 540 h actual (dev 280 / UX 120 / QA 40 / BA 40 / DevOps 30 / architect 30). n=1.

web.why: Generated E2E suites run through the bmad-qat module (https://github.com/Relevant-S/bmad-qat), plus exploratory testing and release verification. ANCHOR: EPP Phase 1 epics 1-9 spent 40 h of QA in total running the suite through bmad-qat, against a manual baseline of roughly 1,200 h — 3.3%. An estimate that assumes the tooling without naming it cannot be checked against the project that produced the rate

mobile_manual.why: Device matrix, store review cycles, and manual regression — the industry default

mobile_mcp_automated.why: This company runs mobile QA through the mobile MCP server, which covers most test cases automatically. Materially cheaper than the industry default, and an estimate that ignores it is wrong in the company's own disfavour

data_ml.why: Validation is empirical and iterative; correctness is statistical rather than binary

overhead_rate._what: Ceremony, demos, client communication and coordination — priced per person per week, NOT as a share of scope. A status call recurs on the calendar, not on the backlog. Charged as a percentage it inherited every scope error the estimate made: a backlog counted ten times over billed ten times the meetings, which turns a granularity mistake into a commercial one. Hours are weeks x people x the rate below; the estimate still reports the implied percentage, as a cross-check rather than as the basis.

low_touch.why: Async updates, a fortnightly demo, an empowered single point of contact

standard.why: Weekly ceremonies, a demo per sprint, a client team that reviews — roughly half a day a week each

high_touch.why: Multiple stakeholders, committee approvals, formal reporting — common in enterprise and public-sector work

uncertainty._what: How the reported band is produced. This is the mechanism that makes false precision structurally impossible: band width is COMPUTED from the input, never chosen.
uncertainty.z_why: Multiplier on the aggregated standard deviation. 1.0 gives roughly a 68% interval, which is honest for a presale figure. Raise to 1.28 for an 80% band when a client wants more confidence — and expect a wider number.

completeness_multiplier.why: Systematic uncertainty from a thin brief is correlated risk, not independent noise, so it widens the band multiplicatively rather than being summed into the variance. At completeness 1.0 the multiplier is 1.0; at 0.5 it is about 1.7; at 0.0 it is 3.0. A two-paragraph brief therefore CANNOT produce a narrow range — the arithmetic forbids it.

uncertainty.model_risk_why: Systematic model uncertainty, as a share of the central estimate, combined in quadrature with the feature-level variance. Summing feature variances in quadrature assumes the errors are independent, and they are not: if the size-band or compression calibration is off, it is off for every feature at once. Quadrature therefore understates the real band, and understates it worst on large scopes — a hundred features would otherwise report a suspiciously tight interval. This floor represents systematic model error, which does not shrink however many features are counted. While the model is UNCALIBRATED it is set high, at 15%; est-calibrate should lower it once backtesting shows how far the model actually lands from actuals.

role_weights._what: How each component's hours divide across roles, and which roles are on the work at all. Each entry carries 'w' and optionally 'requires' — a surface the story must have before that role counts. Roles whose surface is absent are dropped and the survivors renormalise, so the split stays an allocation of the total rather than an adjustment to it. No PM: the Architect absorbs PM responsibilities. The Architect appears ONLY in project-level components — the tech lead does not review individual stories, the developer does, and EPP Phase 1 (480 h delivered across dev/QA/UX/BA) records no architect hours against story work at all. Spreading a fixed architect share over every story was inventing a quarter of the project out of a weight table. A weight may name `requires` (one surface) or `requires_any` (several). `dev` itself is conditional: while it was unconditional it survived renormalisation on an infra-only story and billed a CI pipeline 91% developer. EPP Phase 1: 76 stories, 540 h actual (dev 280 / UX 120 / QA 40 / BA 40 / DevOps 30 / architect 30). n=1.

ba.why: Turning a client sentence into acceptance criteria is BA work

dev.why: The technical half of a story spec — data shape, contract, edge cases — is written by whoever will build it

ux.why: Anything with a visual surface is specified with its interaction, not only the stories where a new design is drawn

dev.why: Steering, correcting and integrating what the agent generates

ux.why: Design runs through build on anything with a visual surface, not only where a new design is being drawn. Keying this on `design` alone put UX at 1.6% of EPP against a measured 22%, because 70 of its 76 stories were frontend and only 15 were tagged design

devops.why: Pipeline, environment and deployment work. With `dev` now also conditional, an infra-only story bills devops alone

dev.why: Story review is developer work, at every tier. The architect/tech lead does not review stories

devops.why: A pipeline or an environment change is reviewed by whoever operates it, and on an infra-only story that is the whole review

dev.why: The loop back into the code is the developer's

devops.why: The loop back into a pipeline or an environment is the operator's

architect.why: Steering the BMad planning workflow, and the PM responsibilities folded into that role

ba.why: Requirements and acceptance criteria across the artefacts

ux.why: The UX artefact and the design decisions the architecture rests on. EPP's design work started in planning and did not stop

architect.why: The architecture and epics are read end to end by the person accountable for them

ba.why: Requirements review against what the client actually asked for

ux.why: Design review of the UX artefact

devops.why: Environments, CI/CD, secrets and observability are the DevOps line — the role this model previously did not have, so the work was billed to developers

dev.why: The application-side wiring a pipeline needs

qa.why: Test execution, triage and release verification

architect.why: Demos, technical client conversations and coordination

ba.why: Ceremony, status and the client communication around scope

dev.why: Standups and demos are not free for the people delivering. Charging ceremony only to the architect and BA put both roughly double their measured share of EPP

phase_map._what: Which BMad delivery phase each component is reported under. This decomposition is what makes the number legible to a client: it maps onto the process actually used rather than an invented breakdown.

calendar._what: Derived, secondary output. Hours are the deliverable; duration depends on a team shape nobody knows at presale.
calendar.hours_per_person_week_why: Six hours of focused delivery a day, five days a week. The remainder is the overhead already priced separately, plus the ordinary friction of a working week.
calendar.max_useful_parallelism_why: Beyond roughly six people on one workstream, coordination cost grows faster than throughput. The critical path, not the headcount, sets the floor on duration.

surfaces._what: Which kinds of work a story touches. This is what decides which roles are on it: a role whose 'requires' surface is absent from the story is dropped from that story's split entirely, so a background job bills no UX and a screen bills no devops. Tagged per story at extraction and confirmable like any other tag. A story with no surfaces tag at all is treated as unknown, and unknown keeps every role in — silence must not quietly discount.
surfaces.backend: Server-side logic, data model, APIs, background jobs, third-party integrations
surfaces.frontend: Screens, client state, forms, tables — implementing a design that already exists
surfaces.design: Visual or interaction design: new screens, a design-system component, an accessibility or microcopy pass
surfaces.infra: Environments, pipelines, deployment, observability, secrets, migrations run against real systems
surfaces.data: Schema migration, import and export, backfills, reporting queries
